name: Nora Kowalski

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me, Nora. I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Anything you tell me stays confidential, so feel free to say both what you'd say in public and what you really think. What does a normal day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I teach Year 4 at Harbour Lane Primary, a city school near the docks, and I lead the lower juniors, so three classes and their teachers. Over half my kids speak another language at home: Polish, Somali, Tagalog, Urdu. My day starts at half seven setting out phonics cards and ends around six after I've checked my team's planning. In between it's thirty eight-year-olds, one of whom always has a loose tooth.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy, and what drains you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The best bit is when a kid who arrived in September with no English reads a whole page out loud in March. The draining bit is the paperwork for every child who needs extra support, which can be ten pages each. I've started using a chatbot now and then to tidy my reports, but only after a friend at another school showed me it was safe. My partner Jonas works nights in A&E, so we eat breakfast together and that's our date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That sounds pretty believable, actually.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a decent tool for tidying a report, and that's about it. In the staffroom we'd laugh about the big promises. I'd probably say good, now spend the money on teaching assistants instead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be fine. Primary teachers are hard to find in this city, so my job is about as safe as jobs get. Jonas and I rent a small flat, we've got around four months saved, and both of us work in places that always need people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing dramatic. I'd keep teaching and leading the team, and keep using the chatbot for the report wording. I'd keep pushing at union meetings for more teaching assistant hours, because that's where the real pressure is in my building.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. A bit cross that so much money went on hype while my kids share one teaching assistant between three classes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the real pressure is teaching assistants. What does that look like on a bad day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our only assistant was with a boy who'd had a meltdown. Last Thursday I had thirty kids, two new arrivals who don't speak English, and I taught fractions with one hand and translated with an app with the other. That's my AI story, really, and it's not a dramatic one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that does worry you in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rent, a bit. Our landlord has hinted at selling, and flats near the school have gone up a lot. But between my pay and Jonas's, we'd find something, even if it's a longer bus ride.

say: AI is a decent tool for **tidying reports**, and that's about it.
Spend the money on **teaching assistants** instead of hype.
think: Primary teachers are **hard to find**, so my job is about as safe as jobs get.
Two steady jobs and about **four months saved** mean money feels manageable.
do: Keep teaching Year 4 and **leading the team** as now.
Keep using the chatbot for **report wording** now and then.
Push at union meetings for more **assistant hours**.
feel: **Calm**, with some **irritation** at money wasted on hype.
S0.quote: Last Thursday I had thirty kids, two new arrivals who don't speak English, and I taught fractions with one hand and translated with an app with the other.
fieldNote: Nora's real pressure is **staffing**, not technology; her AI use is small and practical.
A second steady income from her **nurse partner** keeps her genuinely calm.
Rent is a minor worry, but **landlord selling** is the only real money risk she names.

steps.text: Keep teaching Year 4 and leading the lower juniors team
Keep using a chatbot to tidy support plan wording
Raise teaching assistant hours at the next union meeting

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That one I can picture. Some of it's starting already.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say teachers should get a say in which tools come into schools, and that the time saved should go back to kids, not to bigger classes. In the union I'd want us to write guidance. Online I'd share what's actually working in my classroom, because people need real examples.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think my job is mostly safe, because eight-year-olds need an adult in the room. But the planning and paperwork part of my role, maybe a third of my week, would change. The worry is the head using that to cut my leadership time, or to give me four classes to oversee instead of three.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Once a couple of colleagues had tried them, I'd learn the planning and report tools properly over the first term. I'd help write the union's guidance on how AI is used. And I'd keep saving, maybe adding a bit, because Jonas and I want to buy somewhere in the next few years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy but okay. It's a lot of change at once, and I'm not someone who jumps first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the parents of your kids who don't speak English yet?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the translation tools might actually help them talk to me. Right now I rely on a cousin or an older sibling at pickup. If a translation tool lets the mum of a Somali girl in my class read my notes, that's a good thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said your leadership time might be cut. How would that hit you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Leadership is part of my pay, a small allowance, and it's how I get promoted. If AI does half the planning checks, they might say I don't need the time, and then the allowance is next. It wouldn't be a disaster, but it's my route to deputy head.

say: Teachers should have a **say** in which AI tools come into schools.
Time saved should go **back to kids**, not into bigger classes.
think: My classroom job is **safe** because young children need an adult in the room.
AI could be used to shrink my **leadership time** and the allowance that comes with it.
do: Learn the **planning and report** tools in the first term, once colleagues have tried them.
Help write the union's **AI guidance** for primary schools.
Add a little to savings for a **flat deposit**.
feel: **Uneasy but okay**, because she doesn't like being first to change.
S1.quote: If a translation tool lets the mum of a Somali girl in my class read my notes, that's a good thing.
fieldNote: Nora sees AI as a possible help for **parents** who don't speak English.
Her concern is narrow and specific: the **leadership allowance** and her route to deputy head.
Steady pattern: she'll adopt tools **after colleagues** have proven them.

steps.text: Learn the planning and report tools in the first term
Help write the union's guidance on AI in primary classrooms
Add £100 a month to the flat deposit savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Gosh. That's my current Year 4s still in primary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say young children still need people, and that every school must keep its teachers while we figure this out. I'd join any union campaign going. Online I'd probably be quieter, because I'd honestly not know what to say yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the thinking side of teaching would change overnight: planning, marking, explaining fractions perfectly in Tagalog. What's left is the care side, which is real but might be paid less. My hands-on work as a primary teacher is a hug and a plaster, not machinery, so robots coming later doesn't help much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sign up for the union campaign in the first month and go to the meetings. Jonas and I would stop saving for a flat and just build the cushion, maybe up to six months. I'd look at whether a special needs qualification makes me harder to replace, because those kids need people most.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'm not panicking, because Jonas's job in A&E feels safer, but I'd lie awake running through what my job turns into.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said Jonas's job feels safer. Would you lean on that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, yes, for a while. We'd talk about him picking up extra shifts if my pay dropped. I don't love that, because it's his health on the line with night shifts, but that's what families do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your team, the other two Year 4 teachers?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them we're a team and nobody gets picked off alone. Priya, who's in her first year, is terrified already. I'd want to protect her, and I'm not sure I could.

say: **Young children** still need people, and schools must keep their teachers.
She would back any **union campaign** but stay quieter online.
think: The **thinking side** of teaching would change almost overnight.
Her hands-on work is **care**, which robots won't do, but it may be **paid less**.
do: Join the **union campaign** in the first month.
Pause the flat deposit and build savings towards **six months**.
Look into a **special needs** qualification to stay harder to replace.
feel: **Anxious**, lying awake picturing what her job turns into.
S2.quote: My hands-on work as a primary teacher is a hug and a plaster, not machinery, so robots coming later doesn't help much.
fieldNote: She separates her day into **thinking work** and **care**, and expects pay to follow the care part down.
A partner in **A&E** gives her household some protection, which keeps her below alarmed.
She frets about **Priya**, a first-year colleague, more than her own role.

steps.text: Join the union campaign and its meetings in the first month
Build savings with Jonas up to six months of costs
Put the flat purchase on hold
Enrol on a part-time special needs teaching qualification

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's more like a project than a shock.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say schools have five years to decide what the human teacher is for, and they should start now. I'd want my union to push for every school to plan for it. I'd share that in staff meetings and probably on our teacher forum.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, five years puts me at 32, maybe deputy head by then, and the role would be about people more than paperwork. I think I'd be okay, as long as the care side of teaching is valued. If it's not, I'm in the same spot as the two-year picture, just later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the special needs qualification over two years, part-time. I'd get properly good with the AI tools by year two, once they settle down. And Jonas and I would probably still buy a small flat, but a cheaper one, so we're not stretched when it arrives.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still anxious underneath, but with a plan. Five years of warning is the difference between seeing a wave coming and being knocked over by one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you change first in your team's work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start using the tools for planning so my teachers get time back with the kids now. If I can show the head that the time went into small reading groups, it's harder to cut us later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you think about leaving teaching?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really. I've thought about it, and I'm better with eight-year-olds than with anything else. If I left, it would be to work with children who have additional needs, which is still teaching, really.

say: Schools have **five years** to decide what the human teacher is for.
Every school should start **planning now**, not wait for the deadline.
think: At **32**, possibly deputy head, I'd be fine if **care** is valued.
If care isn't valued, it's the **same problem** as two years, just later.
do: Complete a **special needs** qualification part-time over two years.
Get properly skilled with **AI planning tools** by year two.
Buy a **cheaper flat** with Jonas so they aren't stretched.
S3.quote: Five years of warning is the difference between seeing a wave coming and being knocked over by one.
fieldNote: Extra time lets Nora **plan**, but she still sees pay for care work as uncertain.
She'd use AI to **win back time** for reading groups, making her team harder to cut.
Even under pressure she wants to **stay with children**, not leave teaching.

steps.text: Complete a part-time special needs qualification over two years
Use AI planning tools to free time for reading groups
Buy a cheaper flat with Jonas than first planned

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be 37. That's a whole other life stage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got a decade to get this right, and teachers should lead it. I'd push for training in schools, paid for properly. I'd probably volunteer to run a working group in our trust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think ten years is enough time for me to become someone schools really need: a senior teacher who knows special needs and knows the tools. The worry is more about whether we have kids by then, and what school would look like for them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep teaching and keep moving towards deputy head. I'd learn the tools steadily as they arrive, once they're proven. Jonas and I would buy the flat we planned and maybe start a family in a few years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in a normal way. Like any big change coming, not like a threat to my job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want your own children's school to look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Lots of people. Machines can do the explaining, but a child needs a real adult who knows their name and notices when they're sad. If that's gone, I'd honestly think about teaching my own kids at home some of the time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The teaching assistants. They do the hands-on bits but they're paid least and have least training. If schools cut costs, they go first, and they're often the ones who know the kids best.

say: We have **a decade** to get this right, and **teachers** should lead it.
Schools need **properly paid** training, not courses done after hours.
think: Ten years is time to become a teacher schools **really need**.
The bigger question is **future children** and what school would look like for them.
do: Keep teaching and keep working towards **deputy head**.
Learn new AI tools **steadily** as they're proven.
Buy the planned flat and think about **starting a family**.
feel: **Uneasy** in a normal way, not threatened.
S4.quote: Machines can do the explaining, but a child needs a real adult who knows their name and notices when they're sad.
fieldNote: With ten years, Nora's worry shifts from her job to **her future children's** schooling.
She worries most for **teaching assistants**, the lowest paid people in her school.
Her plans stay close to the career path she already has: **deputy head**.

steps.text: Keep teaching and apply for assistant head within three years
Try each new AI tool once colleagues have tested it
Buy the planned flat with Jonas and plan a first child

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. What would help is time to adjust: guaranteed teacher jobs for a few years, and training paid for by government. And some promise that care work with young children won't be paid like an afterthought.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe the families. A lot of my parents work in warehouses and cleaning, and the robots part would hit them. A kid's learning falls apart when a parent loses work, so if you want to know how schools will cope, look at the parents' jobs too.

headlineQuote: A kid's learning falls apart when a parent loses work, so if you want to know how schools will cope, look at the parents' jobs too.
portrait: Nora is a 27-year-old Year 4 teacher who leads the **lower juniors** at a city primary.
Many of her pupils are **new to English**, and she uses AI now and then for report wording.
She feels calm in AI Plateau, uneasy in Steady Disruption, and **anxious** under fast AGI.
With more warning she plans a **special needs** qualification and a cheaper flat with her partner Jonas.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because care work with young children might end up paid less.
whatWouldHelp: A few years of **guaranteed teacher jobs** and government-paid training.
A promise that **care work** with young children is valued and paid fairly.
